The Lived Experience Collection
Reach the person who lived it — a discovery surface for debut KDP authors
Reader Discovery · Jalen · Jakob · Wanting · Pablo
300,000 years ago
Why would a reader pick up a book by a debut KDP author?
What makes that appealing — and to whom?

The shelf

Every card opens with the author’s own words — membership is attestation plus metadata, so it scales with no editorial headcount.

Ask 1 — would your storefront teams give this shelf a home?

Her own words. The statement is the gate — an attestation, not an Amazon certification.
Observed, not awarded. The badge only says she opted in to reader questions.

Author attestation

The gate is the author’s own statement. No badge, no filter — no store can certify a life.

Ask 2 — what should happen when an attestation is false?

“What if it’s false” is answered one line away — existing report tools, existing policies, no new machinery.

Finished the book? Ask the author

Rosa sees each question.
Nothing appears anywhere unless she publishes it.
No private messaging at any tier.

Ask 3 — what breaks first at scale?

Nothing is public until Rosa publishes it

Answer & publish — it joins her author page
Decline — the question deletes
Leave it — no penalty, no nudges
The loop closes

The person who lived it, answering

Her answer publishes with the question to her author page — where every future reader can see the person behind the book.

Our answer · why it holds

There is a person behind this book.

An AI-written book has no one behind it.
A celebrity memoirist won’t answer you.
This author will.
Author reachability doesn’t sell the book — it pays off after reading

Forced to choose, 16 took the memoir — and 19 said “it depends.”

n = 42 · Of the 19, 12 named the subject — not the author’s fame — as what decides. The shelf merchandises by subject.

Under 55, 12 of 23 said messaging the author makes them more likely to buy. 55 and over: 1 of 15.

“Would being able to message the author — ask a question about the book or their life — change how likely you are to buy it?” · 1 = makes no difference, 5 = much more likely · age and channel are confounded

The hesitation that beat everything: “no way to tell if it’s any good.”

27 of 42 · 18 distrust the reviews that exist · price moved 3.

40 of 42 rated human authorship a 4 or a 5.

n = 42 · nobody below a 3 · “makes no difference” drew zero.

BookNet Canada reads the same way.

Published percentages, external corroboration — our own survey reports counts only.
Trust signal
Let’s talk ARC.
Advance Reader Copies — a debut’s first audience.
Blocked twice: the $50 rule, and review-for-copy.
Vine already does this for products — invited, free, disclosed.
Ask 4 — engagement as metadata, never reviews. Why not books?
